questions.question: What do critics praise about Mad Max: Fury Road?
questions.answer:
Based on the reviews, critics praise several aspects of **Mad Max: Fury Road**:

**Action and spectacle**
- **Ian Nathan (Empire)** highlights the "jaw-dropping action," "barking-mad imagination," and "crackpot humour," noting it's a "triumph" even with Tom Hardy as "the point of calm."
- **Geoff Pevere (Globe and Mail)** calls it an "exercise in relentless, pedal-to-the-metal momentum" that is "savagely pleasurable" and "a double-barrelled shotgun enema straight to the senses."
- **Ty Burr (Boston Globe)** praises it as "one of the most epic action extravaganzas of recent years" and says it's "enough to renew your faith in movies."

**Craft and filmmaking**
- **Brian Tallerico (RogerEbert.com)** admires "a veteran filmmaker working at the top of his game," praising that it pushes forward "without the cheap special effects or paper-thin characters that have so often defined the modern summer blockbuster."
- **Bruce Kirkland (Toronto Sun)** commends the "sensational photography, set design and other technical attributes."

**Vision and tone**
- **Michael O'Sullivan (Washington Post)** credits "Miller's nitro-burning aesthetic vision" and an "entertaining cast."
- **Jake Wilson (Sydney Morning Herald)** appreciates that it's "streamlined and packed with detail, proudly silly and deadly earnest."
- **Ty Burr (Boston Globe)** is struck by "how tender" the film ultimately becomes beneath its epic action.

**Place in the franchise**
- **Cary Darling (Fort Worth Star-Telegram)** says it makes the earlier Mad Max films "seem almost timid by comparison," calling it "a surreal, operatic take on the action movie."
- **Jake Wilson (Sydney Morning Herald)** calls it "the thrill-ride fans have long been waiting for."

In short, critics broadly praise the film's relentless action, technical craftsmanship, Miller's distinctive vision, emotional depth, and its success as a revitalization of the franchise.

questions.question: What did critics dislike about Suicide Squad?
questions.answer:
Critics' complaints about *Suicide Squad* (2016) clustered around several themes:

**Incoherent, patched-together storytelling**
- Marjorie Baumgarten (Austin Chronicle): "Several plot points lack coherence, and inserted flashbacks add to a sense of the film having been fused into shape in the editing room."
- Roxana Hadadi (Chesapeake Family Magazine): despite "some astonishing visuals," overall it is "a sloppy mess."

**Uncompelling characters and weak antagonists**
- Wendy Ide (Observer (UK)): "even a film full of villains needs a credible antagonist, and this is one of the many problems with Suicide Squad."
- Marjorie Baumgarten: "There's no one to root for in this movie, and no one whose prospects we care about."
- Ignatiy Vishnevetsky (AV Club): the idea of nihilist camaraderie "feels like a load of hooey; the characters are often too busy posing to exchange more than a few words at a time."

**Watered-down, generic, and loud rather than sharp**
- Peter Travers (Rolling Stone): director Ayer compromised "his hardcore action bona fides for a PG-13 crowdpleaser that would rather ingratiate than cut deep, or even cut at all."
- Cary Darling (Fort Worth Star-Telegram/DFW.com): "volume is not vision... just another generic superhero action movie."
- Michael O'Sullivan (Washington Post): a "double cop-out" that disappoints both fans of the source material's "grown-up gloom-and-doom aesthetic" and discerning adolescents.

**A missed opportunity**
- Max Weiss (Baltimore Magazine) trashes the film while noting she wants DC fans "to have nice things," pointing to future DC releases instead.

The only real praise in this set came from Hadadi (visuals, Will Smith and Margot Robbie's performances) and Darling ("some entertaining performances").

- **Peter Howell (Toronto Star)**, 3/4: says Cameron "has successfully made a digital blockbuster feel as warm as an old-time movie."
- **Claudia Puig (USA Today)**, 3/4: praises "the grandeur and technical virtuosity of the mythical 3-D universe."
- **Sukhdev Sandhu (Daily Telegraph)**, 3/5: "It's an achievement to make 3D look as good as it does here."
- **Paul Byrnes (Sydney Morning Herald)**, 3/5 (rotten): concedes it is "beautiful" and "a technical wonder," even while calling it "a failure of nerve."

**Caveats about the visuals:**
- **Tom Maurstad (Dallas Morning News)**, 3/5: finds it "impressively seamless" but says "you're never fooled... it looks like a video game," and dismisses the "change the way you look at films" hype.
- **Jake Coyle (Associated Press)**, 2.5/4: calls the effects "clearly revolutionary" but says the film "nevertheless feels unsatisfying."
- **Sandhu** sums up the common reservation: "a triumph of effects over affect" — the characters are "all in 1D." **Puig** similarly calls the characters "one-dimensional," though she adds that "for much of the movie, that hardly matters."

questions.question: What are the main criticisms of Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice?
questions.answer:
## Main criticisms of *Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice* (2016)

**Bloated, sluggish pacing**
- Joshua Rothkopf (Time Out) calls it a "lumbering, dead-on-arrival superhero mélange" and "a $250 million tombstone for a genre in dire need of a break."
- Bruce Kirkland (Toronto Sun) says half the film "is so bloated that it blunts the effect of the good stuff."

**Incoherent, jumbled script**
- Preston Jones (Fort Worth Star-Telegram/DFW.com) describes it as taking "logic, reason and character motivation, tossing it all in a blender and filming the scraps."
- Stephen Whitty (Newark Star-Ledger) says it plays like "a greatest-hits medley of every superhero movie ever made," concluding "none of it convinces."
- Max Weiss (Baltimore Magazine) reduces it to "a blur of pretentious speeches... noisy fight scenes and nonsensical dream sequences."

**Joyless, dour tone**
- Ann Hornaday (Washington Post) says viewers get "down in the mire with protagonists who grimace, scowl and wince their way through heroics with the joyless determination of shift workers making the doughnuts."

**Disappointing action set-pieces**
- Alex Abad-Santos (Vox) argues that since megaton fight scenes are the reason audiences tolerate bad dialogue or logic, "it's an outright tragedy when Batman v Superman's showdowns become as boring as the rest of it."

**A minority positive note:** Steven Rea (Philadelphia Inquirer, 3/4 fresh) found "a gravitas here that even the stalest of comic book tropes can't diminish," praising Snyder's respect for the material and the effects — while Kirkland concedes the first half is "brilliant."

- **Kate Erbland (Film School Rejects), A-**: "An absolute technical marvel in every way possible," with all its technical parts working "in perfect harmony."
- **Sandra Hall (Sydney Morning Herald), 4/5**: "a technical marvel... But Cuaron also knows how suspense works."
- **Rafer Guzman (Newsday), 3/4**: "a rare combination of jaw-dropping special effects and visual artistry" that also works as "slam-bang entertainment."

questions.question: Compare Dunkirk and 1917 as war films.
questions.answer:
**By the numbers:** 1917 edges ahead on both measures — IMDb 8.2 vs. Dunkirk's 7.8, and a critic average of 8.69/10 vs. 8.56/10 (each based on 20 reviews in this database). Both are overwhelmingly fresh (16 of Dunkirk's and 17 of 1917's ratings fall in the 8–10 bucket).

**How critics describe them:**

*Dunkirk (2017)* — War/Action/Drama, seen as a visceral, spectacle-driven experience:
- Rafer Guzman (Newsday): "Few films have stripped war down to its terrifying, thrilling essence as Christopher Nolan's Dunkirk, and few films have turned war into such an overwhelming, almost physical experience."
- Christopher Hooton (Independent (UK)): "an unbelievably assured and thrilling war film. Nolan is at the top of his game."
- Wenlei Ma (News.com.au): "a return to true form... may very well be his best film yet," combining "the clever structure of Memento, the scale and ambition of The Dark Knight."
- Counterpoint: Kevin Maher (Times (UK)), 2/5: "106 clamorous minutes of big-screen bombast that's so concerned with its own spectacle and scale that it neglects to deliver the most crucial element — drama."

*1917 (2019)* — War/History/Thriller, praised as a technical and cinematic achievement:
- Sheraz Farooqi (CinemaDebate): "one of the best war films of all time," citing "the incredible cinematography by Deakins & strong performance by George MacKay."
- Jason Fraley (WTOP): marvels at the single-take approach — "only a rare few have ever dared to shoot a film that appears to unfold in one single take... imagine pulling it off in a war movie."
- Emmanuel Noisette (The Movie Blog): "a phenomenal technical display of a captivating war-time drama. It's visually enthralling."
- Kent Garrison (Mad About Movies Podcast): "not as much a war story as it is a true showcase of the power of moving images... certain it will be talked about for decades."

**In short:** Critics frame both as technically ambitious, immersive war films — Dunkirk as an overwhelming physical experience of spectacle (with one critic faulting its lack of drama), and 1917 as a showcase of cinematography and the one-take technique. The data gives 1917 a slight lead, but the margin is small, and the sources don't settle a definitive verdict.
